title: Bitcoin's $3 Billion Short Squeeze Just Reminded Everyone Why Coinbase Matters
subtitle: Bitcoin ripped past $72,000 on a Treasury-fueled squeeze, short sellers ate $3 billion in losses, and Coinbase — the on-ramp for American crypto — caught the whole wave.
summary: Bitcoin bolted past $72,000 Thursday after the Treasury announced long-term bond buybacks, vaporizing close to $3 billion in short positions — the biggest squeeze since 2021. Coinbase, America's largest crypto exchange, rode it to double-digit gains as Washington's regulatory push added fuel.

links.label: Bitcoin spikes past $72,000 on Treasury-fueled short squeeze (IBD)
Crypto stocks soar alongside Bitcoin as rally reignites

bodyHtml:
Bitcoin woke up angry. It bolted past $72,000 early Thursday — up about 9% on the day and above $70,000 for the first time since early June — after the US Treasury announced long-term bond buybacks. Two months of grinding sideways ended in a single morning, and the crowd that bet against the coin got vaporized. Short sellers lost close to $3 billion in 24 hours, the biggest bitcoin short-bet loss since 2021, with roughly 172,000 traders liquidated, per CoinGlass. When a squeeze gets that violent, it stops being a crypto story and becomes a market story.

So what does that have to do with a stock you can actually buy? Everything. When crypto rips, the fastest, most regulated way to ride it in the US runs through Coinbase. It's the largest American crypto exchange — the place where everyday people and big institutions buy, sell, and store digital assets. Coinbase makes money three ways: trading fees, subscriptions, and its own Base layer-2 blockchain, which has quietly grown into one of the busiest networks in crypto.

Coinbase's stock ripped right alongside Bitcoin — up 9.5% Wednesday, then extending into Thursday morning for double-digit gains across two sessions. Strategy, the biggest corporate bitcoin holder, jumped 9%. Ethereum, the number-two crypto, broke back above $2,000 on a 15% pop. When crypto moves, everything attached to it moves harder, and the whole complex — exchanges, miners, holders — caught a bid.

This wasn't just a market reflex. Washington poured fuel on the fire. The Senate set a vote date for the Clarity Act, the SEC proposed new rules for crypto offerings, and the CFTC held its first Innovation Advisory committee meeting. For an industry that's spent years fighting regulators, that's practically a welcome party. Clear rules are the thing crypto companies have begged for since the beginning — especially an answer to the question that's haunted the market for a decade: which tokens are securities, and which aren't. Coinbase, as the most scrutinized and most compliant exchange in America, is the best-positioned player to cash in when that uncertainty finally lifts.

Here's the part that matters for you. Coinbase isn't just a trading desk; it's the regulated on-ramp for the entire crypto economy. When Bitcoin spikes, fee revenue spikes with it. When institutions decide crypto is real, Coinbase is where most of them open accounts. Retail traders pile in through its consumer app; pension funds and asset managers come through its institutional desk. Both feed the same machine. It's the bellwether — a way to own the toll booth instead of just watching the traffic go by.

The Treasury angle deserves a closer look. Long-term bond buybacks flood the system with liquidity, and liquidity is rocket fuel for risk assets like crypto. Layer on a short squeeze — traders who bet against bitcoin forced to cover at higher prices, pushing it higher still — and you get moves like Thursday's. It's a feedback loop, and Coinbase sits right in the middle of it. Every forced buyback is a trade that runs through an exchange, and in the US, that exchange is usually Coinbase.

There's another layer most headlines miss: Coinbase has been building beyond trading. Its subscription business — custody, stablecoins, staking — generates revenue that doesn't vanish when volume dries up. And Base has grown into a real business line, not a side project. That's why Wall Street keeps calling it the cleanest way to own the crypto cycle without picking individual coins.

None of this means the rally is guaranteed. Bitcoin had been stuck below $70,000 since May, and breaking that ceiling flipped cautious bulls into aggressive buyers — but crypto is volatile, and days like Thursday can reverse as fast as they start. Still, the setup is real: more liquidity, friendlier regulators, and the biggest squeeze in five years. For Coinbase, that's the combination shareholders have been waiting for.

If you've been sitting on the sidelines wondering whether crypto is dead, Thursday was your answer. It's very much alive — and Coinbase is how most of America will play it.
